The Archean Eon. This period, stretching from four point one to two point five billion years ago, witnessed the formation of Earth's first stable continents and the emergence of life itself. The name comes from the Greek word archaios, meaning ancient.

The first solid continental crust formed and began to accumulate into small landmasses called cratons, which became the cores of modern continents. Stromatolites—layered structures built by cyanobacteria—are the oldest known fossils, appearing in the late Archean. The earliest evidence of life in the form of chemical signatures in rocks dates to somewhere between three point eight and three point five billion years ago, making the Archean the period when life on Earth began.

Photosynthesis was already happening by the mid-Archean, though it took another billion years for oxygen to accumulate in the atmosphere during what's called the Great Oxidation Event. The planet was still hot, and impacts from space objects continued, though much less frequently than in the era before the Archean. Archean rocks are rare at the surface today because they have been metamorphosed—altered by heat and pressure—over billions of years.

The Archean connects directly to the hellish Hadean Eon before it, when life had not yet appeared, and to the Proterozoic Eon that followed, marked by the Great Oxidation Event and the rise of oxygen. Stromatolites remain hallmarks of the late Archean period.
